GC.23.stem: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), what did the Supreme Court decide about students' free-speech rights?

choices.text: Schools may ban any student expression that administrators dislike
Students keep their free-speech rights at school unless the expression substantially disrupts learning
The First Amendment does not apply to public-school students
Only teachers, not students, hold free-speech rights at school

GC.23.reteach: Re-read the 'schoolhouse gate' quote; distinguish protected non-disruptive expression from speech that substantially disrupts.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Overstates school authority; Tinker limits, not expands, the power to ban expression.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that students have no First Amendment rights; Tinker holds the opposite.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Right topic but wrong holding; both students and teachers retain rights under Tinker.

GC.23.key_rationale: Tinker held students do not shed their rights at the schoolhouse gate, protecting non-disruptive expression.
GC.23.dok_rationale: Students interpret the meaning of a landmark holding.
GC.23.blooms_rationale: Students explain what the Court decided and its limit.

GC.24.stem: In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), what did the Supreme Court hold about the Second Amendment?

choices.text: That only the military may lawfully own weapons
That the amendment applies only to state militias
That states may ban all firearms within their borders
That the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms

GC.24.reteach: Re-read the Heller quote on an 'individual right'; then trace how McDonald v. Chicago applied it to the states.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that only the military may bear arms; Heller recognized an individual right.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: The militia-only reading is the interpretation Heller rejected.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralizes state power; Heller struck down a strict handgun ban.

GC.24.key_rationale: Heller held that the Second Amendment confers an individual right to keep and bear arms.
GC.24.dok_rationale: Students interpret the outcome of a landmark case.
GC.24.blooms_rationale: Students explain the ruling rather than merely name the case.

GC.25.stem: The exclusionary rule, established in Mapp v. Ohio (1961), provides that —

choices.text: evidence obtained through an illegal search cannot be used against a defendant in court
police may search a home without a warrant in most situations
a suspect must answer every question police ask
criminal trials may be conducted in secret

GC.25.reteach: Connect the exclusionary rule to the 4th Amendment; use a short scenario of an illegal search and ask what happens to the evidence.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts the 4th Amendment, which the exclusionary rule enforces.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses the 4th Amendment rule with the 5th Amendment right to remain silent.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception unrelated to the exclusionary rule; trials are public under the 6th Amendment.

GC.25.key_rationale: Mapp's exclusionary rule bars illegally obtained evidence from being used in court.
GC.25.dok_rationale: Students interpret the effect of a rule established by a case.
GC.25.blooms_rationale: Students explain the consequence the exclusionary rule creates.

GC.26.stem: Why is Brown v. Board of Education (1954) considered a turning point in interpreting the Equal Protection Clause?

choices.text: It upheld the 'separate but equal' doctrine from Plessy v. Ferguson
It removed the Equal Protection Clause from the 14th Amendment
It ruled that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal,' ending lawful school segregation
It applied only to private colleges, not public schools

GC.26.reteach: Contrast Plessy (1896) and Brown (1954); underline how the same clause was read in opposite ways.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Reverses the ruling; Brown overturned, not upheld, 'separate but equal.'

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that a case can delete a constitutional clause.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Wrong scope; Brown concerned public schools, not private colleges.

GC.26.key_rationale: Brown held segregated schools inherently unequal, overturning Plessy's 'separate but equal.'
GC.26.dok_rationale: Students interpret how a ruling changed a clause's meaning.
GC.26.blooms_rationale: Students explain the significance of the Brown decision.

GC.27.stem: What does Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibit?

Discrimination based on sex in education programs that receive federal funds
The teaching of American history in public schools
Voting by citizens under the age of 21

distractor_tags.label: C

distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses Title IX with the 26th Amendment's voting age.

formA.stem: A public high school suspends a student for silently wearing an armband to protest a government policy, and the protest caused no disruption. Based on Tinker v. Des Moines, how should a court most likely rule?

choices.text: For the student, because non-disruptive symbolic speech is protected at school
For the school, because students give up their rights at the schoolhouse gate
For the school, because all forms of student protest are banned
For the student, because the First Amendment allows no limits on speech

formA.reteach: Apply the Tinker test to the fact pattern: was the speech symbolic and non-disruptive? Practice with additional armband/T-shirt scenarios.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Tinker's core holding that students keep their rights.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralizes; Tinker protects non-disruptive protest, not bans all protest.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Uses a partly-true idea (speech is protected) but ignores the 'substantial disruption' limit.

formA.key_rationale: Tinker protects silent, non-disruptive symbolic speech, so the student should prevail.
formA.dok_rationale: Students apply a precedent to a new fact pattern to predict the outcome.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students carry out the Tinker rule in an unfamiliar scenario.

formA.stem: The principle that a protection in the Bill of Rights is applied to state and local governments through the 14th Amendment is called —

choices.text: judicial review
symbolic speech
incorporation
original jurisdiction

formA.reteach: Define incorporation with McDonald v. Chicago as the example; map how a federal right becomes binding on the states.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Judicial review is the power to void laws, not the process of applying rights to states.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Symbolic speech is a First Amendment concept, not the state-application doctrine.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Original jurisdiction concerns which court hears a case first.

formA.key_rationale: Incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to the states via the 14th Amendment.
formA.dok_rationale: Students match a defined process to the correct concept.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning of the incorporation concept.

formA.stem: Police arrest a suspect and begin questioning her without telling her she has the right to remain silent and to a lawyer. Based on Miranda v. Arizona, what is the most likely consequence?

choices.text: Her statements are automatically valid because she was under arrest
Her statements may be excluded from trial because she was not warned of her rights
She permanently loses her right to a jury trial
The arrest violates the Second Amendment

formA.reteach: Apply Miranda step by step: no warning before custodial questioning means statements can be suppressed. Use a short arrest scenario.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Miranda; being under arrest does not validate unwarned statements.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralizes a consequence; Miranda affects statements, not the right to trial.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Confuses amendments; Miranda involves the 5th Amendment, not the 2nd.

formA.key_rationale: Under Miranda, statements from unwarned custodial questioning may be excluded.
formA.dok_rationale: Students apply a precedent to a scenario to predict the legal result.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students carry out the Miranda rule in an unfamiliar case.

formA.stem: How can the same Equal Protection Clause have supported segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) yet ended it in Brown v. Board of Education (1954)?

choices.text: Congress rewrote the clause between the two cases
Plessy did not actually involve the Equal Protection Clause
The two rulings interpreted different amendments
The Supreme Court reinterpreted the clause's meaning over time

formA.reteach: Trace the change in interpretation across 1896–1954; emphasize that constitutional meaning is decided by people over time.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that a clause was rewritten; the text stayed the same.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Plessy did rest on equal protection, so this is factually wrong.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Both cases interpreted the 14th Amendment, not different amendments.

formA.key_rationale: The same clause yielded opposite results because the Court reinterpreted it over time.
formA.dok_rationale: Students analyze how interpretation, not text, changed between rulings.
formA.blooms_rationale: Students break down the cause of two opposite outcomes from one clause.

formB.stem: The Supreme Court has said the Second Amendment right is 'not unlimited.' What does that mean?

choices.text: Governments may still regulate who may carry firearms, and where and how
Only the military may lawfully own weapons
States may ban all firearms outright
The amendment does not protect any individual at all

formB.reteach: List examples of allowed regulation the Court signaled in Heller; distinguish 'protected right' from 'unlimited right.'

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Heller's individual-right holding.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralizes; a total ban conflicts with the recognized right.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Contradicts Heller, which found an individual right.

formB.key_rationale: 'Not unlimited' means firearms may still be regulated as to who, where, and how.
formB.dok_rationale: Students interpret the meaning of a qualifying phrase from the Court.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students explain what a limited right permits governments to do.

formB.stem: The requirement that the state provide a lawyer to a defendant who cannot afford one comes from which Supreme Court case?

choices.text: Mapp v. Ohio
Gideon v. Wainwright
Miranda v. Arizona
Brown v. Board of Education

formB.reteach: Match each accused-rights case to its amendment: Mapp (4th), Gideon (6th), Miranda (5th); quiz with the case-to-right pairing.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Mapp established the exclusionary rule, not the right to counsel.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Miranda concerns warnings and silence, not appointed counsel.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Brown is an equal-protection case, unrelated to right to counsel.

formB.key_rationale: Gideon v. Wainwright guaranteed appointed counsel to defendants who cannot afford one.
formB.dok_rationale: Students recall which case established a specific right.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students retrieve the correct case from memory.

formB.stem: The 14th Amendment's guarantee that no state may 'deny to any person… the equal protection of the laws' was the constitutional basis for which ruling?

choices.text: Schenck v. United States
District of Columbia v. Heller
Brown v. Board of Education
Miranda v. Arizona

formB.reteach: Link the Equal Protection Clause to Brown; contrast with cases resting on other amendments (Schenck-1st, Heller-2nd, Miranda-5th).

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Schenck rests on the First Amendment, not equal protection.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Heller rests on the Second Amendment, not equal protection.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Miranda rests on the Fifth Amendment, not equal protection.

formB.key_rationale: Brown v. Board rested on the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
formB.dok_rationale: Students connect a constitutional clause to the case it grounded.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students construct meaning by matching clause to ruling.

formB.stem: Why do many scholars today point to Korematsu v. United States (1944) as a cautionary example rather than a model to follow?

choices.text: It created Title IX and later proved unnecessary
It expanded voting rights too quickly
It ended school segregation before the country was ready
It upheld the wartime incarceration of Japanese Americans, showing how liberty can be sacrificed to claimed security

formB.reteach: Discuss the security-vs-liberty tension using Korematsu; have students judge why it is now condemned, citing the facts.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Korematsu had nothing to do with Title IX.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Korematsu narrowed rights; it did not expand voting rights.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Ending segregation was Brown, not Korematsu.

formB.key_rationale: Korematsu is a warning because it upheld incarcerating Japanese Americans in the name of security.
formB.dok_rationale: Students judge why a ruling is condemned, weighing liberty against security.
formB.blooms_rationale: Students evaluate the case against a criterion of protected rights.
